newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Fiat sees higher profits in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fiat sees higher profits in 1997.

text.p: Italy's largest private industrial group Fiat on Monday forecast "considerable higher" operating profits for 1997 driven by the success of a national car buying incentive scheme in Italy started this year.

Group chairman Cesare Romiti told the group's annual shareholders meeting that margins in Fiat's car business had started to improve in March and this together with increased sales would lead to better operating profits in 1997.
"Auto margins in the first quarter were much better in March because the incentive scheme took some time to take off, and April and May also showed this positive impact," he said.

In 1996, Fiat's operating income from its industrial activities was 2.1 trillion lire ($1.24 billion) on sales of around 78 trillion lire, but net profits were boosted by extraordinary gains from the partial flotation of New Holland and the sale of fund management arm Prime to insurance giant Generali.

For this year, Romiti reiterated his message last month that group 1997 sales would rise around 15 percent to 90 trillion lire from the previous year while its income before taxes should not fall short of 1996's 3.8 trillion lire level.

Fiat's managing director Paola Cantarella said its carmaking division Fiat Auto would see sales up nine trillion lire driven higher by the incentive scheme in Italy and also increased sales in the rest of Europe and South America.
Both Romiti and Cantarella stressed the importance of the car incentive scheme continuing in Italy.
The scheme, started in January and set to run to September, allows owners of cars older than 10 years to trade their vehicles in for scrapping in return for a price discount on a new car.

Romiti added "The government must devise something for the incentives to continue", while Cantarella added that there should be a "soft landing" for the Italian car market after the incentive scheme is scheduled to finish in September.

Cantarella said the Italian car market in 1998 risked falling back to its 1996 level of 1.7 million cars if the scheme was not continued. He saw the 1997 market at around two million after the Italian car market crashed from well over two million in 1992 and stuck at around 1.7 million for 1993-1996.
The Italian car market has risen sharply this year due to incentives but there are signs that orders may now be slowing.
Cantarella added that due to extra added value added tax and new car registration tax, the scheme actually gave a net benefit to the Italian government of around 477 billion lire.

At the meeting Romiti released divisional figures for the first few month of 1997 and added, "The results achieved thus far...point to an overall improvement in the group's operating and financial performance compared with 1996."
He added the group's financial position should be positive in 1997, indicating it would move into a net cash position.

Looking at the group's divisions, Romiti said the western European car market slipped 4.2 percent on a unit sales basis in the first five months of 1997, and would have been worse except for a 27.9 percent gain in Italy, boosted by incentives.

Fiat Auto sales rose 8.2 percent to 1.12 million cars worldwide in the first five months, with the only area of weakness being western Europe, excluding Italy, where Fiat sales were off 18.1 percent due to weak consumer demand.

Romiti said the results in the first five months pushed Fiat's market share in Europe to 12.6 percent to move Fiat from fifth position in the European car industry league in 1996 to second in 1997 behind leader Volkswagen.

In commercial vehicles, Fiat's Iveco heavy trucks units saw sales off 8.8 percent in the first four months of 1997 at 37,900 units due to depressed markets and its share of the European truck market declined to 18.4 percent from 20 percent.

Fiat's 69-percent owned New Holland agricultural and industrial machinery maker saw tractor sales in the first four months of 1997 up 16.1 percent at 7,200 units, with the European tractor market increasing slightly while the market remained buoyant in north America. $=1,696
